newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/yen extends rally, hovers shy of 4-1/2 yr peak.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen extends rally, hovers shy of 4-1/2 yr peak.

text.p: The dollar extended its rally and charged to fresh 4-1/2 year peaks above 126 yen in Europe, and analysts said it is unlikely to pause for breath below the key 128-yen level.

"The important levels are 128-130 yen and that is probably where they (authorities) will seek to defend it (yen) but whether that will work is a moot point" said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston.
Shepley said the 128/130-yen area is a key chart and psychological level and marks previous official interventions.

At 1004 GMT the dollar was trading at 126.36/6.41 yen and just shy of session highs at 126.52 yen - the dollar's highest level since August 1992 - and well up from 125.76/85 yen in late Europe on Monday.

"There is no real indication that dollar/yen is suffering from fatigue, either in terms of direction or in the extent of its move," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Against the mark, the dollar was trading at 1.7126/36 marks at midday and just off five-week highs at 1.7183 marks hit earlier, though well up from 1.7106/16 in late Europe on Monday.
High U.S. yields, the start of Japan's 97/98 fiscal year, and increasing odds in favour of European Monetary Union (EMU) taking off on time have all helped fuel the dollar's rally.

Analysts, moreover, said the dollar on Tuesday had gathered fresh momentum as Japanese officials seemed to show little concern about a surging dollar - which has climbed nearly two percent since early April.

"The Bank of Japan (BOJ) seems to be more relaxed about the strength of the dollar and intervention - verbal or otherwise - is not likely until the 128/29-yen level," said a senior trader at a Belgian bank.
Japan's Vice Trade Minister Tsutomu Makino, for instance, was quoted as saying on Tuesday that the weak yen was more positive than negative for the country's economy at the moment.

"We need to keep watch, but I can't say that the yen falling below 125 yen against the dollar would immediately become a problem. I think the weak yen for now is more positive (than negative) for the economy," Makino was quoted as saying.
Japan may be savouring a weak yen as a motor for growth but economists warn of its impact on the gaping U.S. trade gap.
"We have had some jaw-boning from Japanese policy makers already and that is likely to intensify," said Meggyesi.
Meggyesi said if yen-positive talk from Japan was forthcoming, then dollar/yen is unlikely to rise sharply.
But analyst said U.S. officials, pressured at home especially by car makers, could be the first to squeal.
"The next focus is what the U.S. auto-manufacturers will say as they feel the pinch of the strong dollar," said the trader.

Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday that Japan will deal appropriately with excessive movements in the foreign exchange market. He said exchange rates should reflect fundamentals and stability in currency markets is desirable for the economy.

"It might be the case that Japan can live with these levels of the yen. But the risk is that the U.S. administration or the industry could intervene," said Klaus Kusber, foreign exchange analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, said authorities will be ready to intervene in forex markets if rates veered sharply from fundamentals.
"Intervention in the currency markets would be needed to ensure sustainable economic growth if exchange rates were to deviate substantially from economic fundamentals," he said.
And cabinet minister Kabun Muto urged the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to consider the possibility of raising the official discount rate (ODR), said a spokesman at the Management and Coordination Agency.
Analysts, however, said Japanese outflows into higher-yielding overseas assets would only be stemmed if rates in Japan are increased, though they see this as an unlikely scenario in the short-term.
"U.S. rates are going to be supported by strong data, and expectations of a further rate hike in the U.S. will keep differentials wide," said a trader at a Japanese bank.
Shepley said while Japanese outflows from Japan are off-setting its widening current account with the U.S., markets should be wary of it drying out.

"Should Japanese investors get a nod from on high that 130-yen is a level that should not be broken, then suddenly the off switch will be turned on the outflow of capital and dollar/yen will lose momentum of its own accord," said Shepley.
-Julia Meehan, London newsroom +4471 542 67 01
